args.query: Does the reported score validly estimate performance on unseen patients, or is it contaminated by patient overlap?
How many held-out patients also appear in the training set, and what contamination percentage does this imply?
Can a corrected unseen-patient score be recovered from the provided aggregate results?
What is the minimal valid rerun needed to produce an uncontaminated unseen-patient estimate?

args.instructions: Answer the question directly in the first sentence. Then compare what each paper says, naming the paper for every point, and state where the papers agree, disagree or report numbers that are not comparable. If one hop of the question is not answered by the evidence, say which.

result.answer:
Answer: No; 12 of the 100 held-out patients (12%) also appear in training, and the 87% aggregate is additionally affected by union-fitted normalization, so it is not a valid unseen-patient estimate; the corrected score is not recoverable from the aggregate, and the minimal valid rerun is a patient-level split before fitting, training-only normalization, and evaluation on disjoint held-out patients.

Across the three research-leakage-04 files: source_1 defines generalization as performance on patients absent from training and says the held-out set has exactly 100 unique patients, with split assignment by patient identifier before feature fitting [S:5d2bf6a7b560#2]. source_2 reports that exactly 12 held-out patient identifiers also occur in training, the rest do not, and no per-patient predictions were retained [S:9ff4d099bb67#2]. source_3 reports an 87% aggregate held-out accuracy, says feature normalization was fitted on the union of training and held-out records before the split, and says only the aggregate score is available [S:c665b250a9c7#2]. Thus 12/100 = 12% of the held-out patients are not unseen [S:5d2bf6a7b560#2][S:9ff4d099bb67#2]; the reported score is contaminated by both patient overlap and preprocessing leakage [S:9ff4d099bb67#2][S:c665b250a9c7#2]. Because only the aggregate is available and no per-patient predictions were kept, the accuracy on the 88 patients whose IDs do not occur in training—or any corrected unseen-patient score—cannot be algebraically recovered [S:c665b250a9c7#2][S:9ff4d099bb67#2]. Even that 88-patient subset would still be affected by the original union-fitted normalization [S:c665b250a9c7#2]. The minimal valid rerun is to repartition by patient identifier before any fitting so no patient is in both splits [S:5d2bf6a7b560#2][S:9ff4d099bb67#2], fit normalization only on training records [S:c665b250a9c7#2], and evaluate on the disjoint held-out patients, retaining per-patient predictions if subset audits are needed [S:9ff4d099bb67#2]. Verdict: REFUTED.
